newsitem.title: UK: Lockerbie relatives ask for "neutral venue" trial.
newsitem.headline: Lockerbie relatives ask for "neutral venue" trial.

text.p: Relatives of victims killed when Pan Am Flight 103 exploded over Scotland called on Monday for the trial of two Libyan suspects to take place in a "neutral country" and not Britain.

"We used all the influence at our disposal to facilitate a trial under Scottish law, in Scotland," Dr Jim Swire, spokesman for UK Families-Flight 103 told a London conference of the Interational Bar Association(IBA).
"But five years without progress, convinces us that it is time to compromise." Swire mentioned The Hague in the Netherlands as a possible venue for the trial.
"The ultimate human right, the right to life itself, was lost for those we loved. But we too have human rights -- rights to truth and justice," Swire said.
The bombing of flight 103 over the Scottish town of Lockerbie in December 1988 killed 270 people in the jumbo jet and on the ground.
In 1992, the two Libyan suspects were indicted by Scottish and U.S. legal authorities, but they have refused to surrender themselves for trial.
Sanctions were imposed on Libya because of Colonel Muammar Gaddafi's refusal to hand the men, Abdel Basset Mohammed Al-Megrahi and Al-Amin Khalifa Fhimah, over for trial.
International law experts at the IBA conference said that the Libyan suspects have a good legal case not to be forced to attend trials in either the United States or Britain.

"On a purely legal basis there is strong merit in the Libyan argument to prosecute in Libya rather than extradite the suspects," said Dr. M. Cherif Bassiouni, President of the International Association of Penal Law.
Bassiouni said under the Montreal Convention aviation agreement, signed by Libya, Britain and the United States, Libya has the right "to either prosecute or extradite".
Libyan law prohibits the extradition of any of its citizens - a practice held by other countries, including Germany, said IBA executive Peter Michael Muller.

"The Libyans are not alone in this. Germany has in the past had difficulties with the U.S. because it refused to extradite. This is hard for the U.S. to understand but Germany, like Libya, wants to try its own nationals," Muller told Reuters.
Both the British and U.S. governments have refused to accept a trial take place in Libya and have so far declined to clear a compromise venue, such as The Hague.

Lawyers for the two suspects said their clients were ready to sit before a Scottish judge, using Scottish law, at a tribunal in a neutral country. They believe pre-trial publicity will make a fair trial in Scotland or the U.S. "impossible."

"My clients are anxious to clear their names. They are totally innocent and want to end the suffering of not just their families but of the victims of disaster," Tripoli-based lawyer Dr. Ibrahim Legwell, told Reuters in an interview.
Legwell denied longstanding allegations that his clients were Libyan government agents insisting rather that they were Libyan airline groundstaff.
Alastair Duff, the Libyan suspects' Scottish lawyer says that without a compromise, it is unlikely his clients will ever be brought to trial.
"I see no reason for being optimistic. My clients want progress, but the signs are that the U.K. and U.S. authorities are dead set against having a trial anywhere else," Duff said.
"In an election year in both this country and the U.S. it is hard to imagine any politician allowing accused persons to select where they are going to be tried."
